slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by making the chapter feel like a construction project rather than a list of formulas. We already know how to talk about congruent segments, order, and triangles; now those tools are asked to manufacture arithmetic. The key promise is that coordinates will not be imported from algebra but recovered from geometry by choosing a unit and proving the operations behave like a field.

slides.label: Chapter Question
slides.notes: The guiding question should be heard literally: before coordinates are available, the only legitimate inputs are points, segments, congruence, betweenness, and constructions. Addition is intuitive because one can place segments end to end. Multiplication is the deeper move, because it uses similarity to turn a two-dimensional construction into a one-dimensional product.

slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Use this as the table of contents for the lecture. The students should see that the chapter is not merely defining formulas in a geometric costume; every operation has an invariance issue that must be checked. The route also helps separate the easy intuition of measuring a segment from the harder claim that the resulting measurements obey field arithmetic.

slides.label: Segment Addition
slides.notes: This construction is deliberately simple, because it establishes the pattern for the rest of the chapter. A segment is represented by a placement on a chosen ray, but the arithmetic object is the congruence class rather than the drawing. The proof obligation is to show that replacing either summand by a congruent copy changes only the representative, not the resulting sum.

slides.label: Order And Positivity
slides.notes: Pause here to connect order with the earlier axioms of betweenness. The statement that one segment is smaller than another has a geometric witness: after placing both from the same origin, one endpoint lies between the origin and the other endpoint. This matters later because an ordered field is not just a field with labels; its positive cone must agree with the geometry of the ray.

slides.label: Multiplication Machine
slides.notes: This is the central visual of the lecture, so do not rush it. The point is not that the drawing literally computes a decimal product, but that similarity transfers the ratio determined by the unit triangle to a larger triangle whose base is the segment a. The formula becomes meaningful only after the unit has been chosen and after we know the parallel construction is independent of incidental drawing choices.

slides.label: Division
slides.notes: Division is best presented as the same machine run backward. If multiplication sends a base length through a fixed ratio determined by b, division asks which base length would produce the desired output a. This also clarifies why the zero segment is excluded: the similarity setup collapses when the controlling segment cannot define a nondegenerate ratio.

slides.label: Algebra Laws
slides.notes: This slide identifies the proof work that arithmetic hides. Addition laws mostly follow from the one-dimensional picture, while multiplication laws require repeated use of similarity and parallel transfer. Distributivity is the conceptual bridge: it says that scaling a whole concatenated segment agrees with scaling its pieces and then concatenating the outputs.

slides.label: Unit Choice
slides.notes: Treat the unit as a gauge choice, because that language helps students distinguish coordinate labels from geometric facts. A longer unit makes the same physical segment receive a smaller coordinate, but the segment itself and its incidence relations have not changed. The later coordinate theorem is credible only if the construction respects that separation between scale-dependent names and scale-independent geometry.

slides.label: Coordinate Axis
slides.notes: This is the first moment where the construction begins to look like ordinary analytic geometry. Emphasize that the coordinate is not attached to a point in isolation; it is attached to a point after choosing an origin, an orientation, and a unit. The sign convention packages the two rays through the origin into one ordered arithmetic line.

slides.label: Coordinate Plane
slides.notes: The coordinate plane construction is a translation device. Parallel projection lets one ask two one-dimensional questions about a point: where does it land on the first axis, and where does it land on the second axis. The important invariant is that lines should become linear equations over the constructed field, so incidence in the plane becomes algebraic incidence in coordinates.

slides.label: Line Equations
slides.notes: This slide states the first serious validation target for coordinates. If the construction is faithful, a straight geometric line should not turn into an arbitrary set of pairs; it should be described by one linear equation over the segment field. This gives students a concrete reason for all the earlier arithmetic checks: without distributivity and order compatibility, the line dictionary would fail.

slides.label: Proof Scaffold
slides.notes: Use this as a proof map rather than a theorem to memorize. Each arrow marks a preservation claim: operations must be well-defined, line coordinates must respect signed order, plane coordinates must reflect parallel projection, and linear equations must capture geometric lines. The final coordinate model is convincing only because incidence and betweenness have been carried through the entire chain.

slides.label: Similarity Dependencies
slides.notes: This slide gives students a unifying mental model. Similar triangles are not a separate topic inserted into arithmetic; they are the mechanism that transports ratios without already having numerical multiplication. When the same pattern appears in product, quotient, and coordinate projection, students can see why the chapter sits after similarity rather than before it.

slides.label: Common Mistakes
slides.notes: These warnings are meant to stop three very natural shortcuts. Students who already know analytic geometry may silently import real-number length, but that would erase the chapter's purpose. The other two mistakes are more subtle: treating the unit as invisible, and accepting one clean drawing as a proof of well-definedness.

slides.label: Worked Example
slides.notes: The example intentionally uses familiar integer marks, but phrase them as repeated unit segments rather than pre-existing numbers. The unit triangle has base one and height two; scaling the base to three forces the height to scale to six by similarity. This gives the audience a quick sanity check for the more abstract construction without replacing the proof.

slides.label: Exercise
slides.notes: Let students identify that the construction has lost similarity, so ratios are no longer being transferred faithfully. The first casualty is well-defined multiplication, and distributivity will also become suspect because different drawings of what should be the same product can produce different outputs. The exercise is useful because it makes the parallel condition feel like a mathematical necessity rather than a drafting preference.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter's central transformation. The result is not just a convenient way to label points; it is a structural bridge from synthetic Euclidean geometry to analytic geometry over an ordered field. This prepares the next chapter because area will need both geometric invariance and arithmetic control, especially when comparing dissections, coordinates, and measurement.
